title_original: With Her Miu Miu Commission in Paris, Filmmaker Alice Diop Offers a Much-Needed Space for Healing
editorial_title_zh: 电影导演爱丽丝·迪奥普携手 Miu Miu 在巴黎推出委任创作，为疗愈提供了一片备受期盼的空间
editorial_excerpt_zh: 此次委任创作是对她长期以来关于跨越时空黑人女性形象呈现之研究的延伸。

"translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的背景很大程度上是在人类学电影领域或与之相关的人类学领域。在大学里，我学的是人类学和历史学，正是这些把我引向了电影。我们在我的视频装置开头看到的影像，是一位电影档案管理员为我找到的。我在筹备下一部剧情长片时雇用了他来寻找这些影像，那部电影将改编自米歇尔·莱里斯（Michel Leiris）的《幻影非洲》（Phantom Africa），这部文本确实是法国人类学和当代人类学的基石。它还揭示了这门在 1930 年代初露端倪的学科在多大程度上与殖民统治息息相关，以及人类学和人类学研究如何表现出一种捕获他者的意志。因此，这位与我合作的出色档案管理员找到了这些来自法国、德国和意大利人类学探险队的影像。《无题》中还收录了由阿尔贝·卡恩（Albert Kahn）资助的项目《地球档案馆》（The Archives of the Planet）以及早期卢米埃尔（Lumière）电影的节选。其中还有一些私人档案影像，以及一些 1930 年代的电影，例如《刚果之旅》（Voyage au Congo）。因此，它真正提供的是从 20 世纪初到 20 世纪中期这类影像的全景，我认为它们揭示了一种关于他者的集体想象。我作为电影导演的目光正是在对抗这些影像的过程中发展起来的。这些影像展示和呈现黑人女性的方式告诉我，我是如何被构建的，并在很大程度上揭示了我为何成为一名电影导演——为了涤荡和疗愈我自己。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": Mbakam）的电影《德尔芬的祈祷》（Les prières de Delphine）[2021]。其中包含克里斯·马克（Chris Marker）电影中的一些影像，它们更具模棱两可性，此外还有佩德罗·科斯塔（Pedro Costa）的电影《维塔利娜·瓦雷拉》（Vitalina Varela）[2019]中的影像。这些都是黑人女性在电影中的出场，她们被赋予了尊重与尊严——这些影像帮助我疗愈，并帮助我更精准地确立了我作为电影制作人的目光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "无论是《维纳斯的碎片》还是你的剧情长片《圣奥梅尔》（Saint Omer），你在音乐的使用上都极为克制却十分精准。但在《无题》（[Sans Titre]）中，音乐贯穿了整部电影。你为什么选择以这种方式来处理电影的配乐？", "translated": true}, {"type": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/miumiu-empty_space-press-261019-7_72_16x9.jpg?w=400", "alt": "紫色地面上一组座位附近的两个讲台。", "caption": "爱丽丝·迪奥普为 Miu Miu 创作的委任作品《慰藉之手》（Geste de Consolation）。图片由 Miu Miu 提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我认为让安吉尔和内伊玛加入并参与这部电影创作是一个正确的直觉，因为这里有一个非常棘手的问题：如何使用这些影像，包括如何让黑人女性暴露在这些影像之中。我不想以一种会伤害她们的方式再次向她们展示这种暴力。这是一个非常棘手的问题，我发现唯一的解决方法其实是让音乐为我们提供一个观点，来决定我希望人们如何看待这些影像。由此产生的音乐是[一段录音]：黑人女性看着这些影像，哭泣、祈祷、安慰、复仇——这确实就是发生的事情。内伊玛和安吉尔和我一起去了工作室。我们架起了屏幕。我们三个人一起观看了这些影像。我们哭了，然后她们以非常有机的方式针对影像进行了作曲。这就像是一场现场电影音乐会——她们伴随着这些档案影像进行现场表演。这是一次极其震撼的体验。然后第二天，我将音乐剪辑到影像中，但[剪辑]非常少，因为同样地，它是如此的有机。人声、哭泣声、安吉尔的呼唤声、她的单簧管以及内伊玛的钢琴之间的关系——它是如此精准。这让我意识到，这实际上是唯一可能的画外音，也是让观众直面这些影像的唯一途径。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/miumiu-empty_space-press-261019-14_72_16x9.jpg?w=400", "alt": "棕色墙面上一个人在镜子中端详自己的影像。", "caption": "爱丽丝·迪奥普为 Miu Miu 创作的委任作品《慰藉之手》（Geste de Consolation），其中展出了扎内尔·姆霍利（Zanele Muholi）的作品。图片由 Miu Miu 提供", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你如何处理耶拿宫（Place d’Iéna）的建筑来完成这项委任创作，这与扎内尔·姆霍利和西蒙娜·利（Simone Leigh）的作品以及表演项目之间有何关联？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "嗯，它就像是一条轨迹或一条路径。重要的是，对展出的每一件对象都倾注了精准的关注。同时，我希望让访客拥有自由，能够从一个空间移动到另一个空间。这确实是一条从照片通往雕塑的路径。我无法预测访客们将会体验到什么，因为这是非常个人的。但其核心理念是，这是一条通往关怀、通往疗愈的叙事路径。在这一条经过深思熟虑的轨迹上出现的每一件对象之间的关系都是精准的。我们从扎内的照片开始，我认为这就是我希望人们对这些影像抱持的视角，接着是带有视频的装置空间，这是一个充满暴力并唤起对慰藉之需求的场所。然后我们来到了表演空间，这些女性直接走出了画框，展现出最本真的自我。她们宣扬自己做自己的权利，转瞬间，她们便带着全部的美丽与力量呈现在我们面前。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "For a few days this week, filmmaker Alice Diop has created a space for healing. For this year’s Miu Miu commission during Art Basel Paris, she has transformed the Place d’Iéna into a large-scale installation title Geste de Consolation (Gesture of Consolation).", "links": [{"text": "Alice Diop", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/alice-diop/"}, {"text": "Miu Miu", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/miu-miu/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The journey begins with Zanele Muholi’s Bona, Charlottesville, Virginia (2015), from the “Somnyama Ngonyama (Hail the Dark Lioness)” series. In the black-and-white photograph, we see the artist looking at themself in a mirror, but her face is only visible through their reflection. Beyond this is a new film by Diop, title [Sans titres] , which begins with excerpts from ethnographic films of African women, depicted as the other, and ending with shots that show empowered Black women."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Further along is “Chambre à soi” (Living Room and Library), which Diop describes as a “living room for a thinking Black woman—a space of pause, learning and encounter. Libraries have long been quietly radical spaces of Black political imagination.” In a space modeled after Diop’s own office, with rugs inspired by the visual motifs of Gee’s Bend quilter Mary Lee Bendolph, visitors can take time to read through books by Christina Sharpe, Virginia Woolf, and Jean Genet and peruse monographs on Otobong Nkanga, Deana Lawson, Henry Taylor, Chantal Akerman, Mona Hatoum, Jacqueline de Jong, Marcel Duchamp, and more."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Between the “Chambre à soi” and Simone Leigh ’s towering 2020–21 sculpture Sentinel (Mami Wata) , which concludes the journey, is a performance space, whose offerings will alternate between an embodied performance Angel Bat Dawid and the Sistazz of the Nitty Gritty and Nadia Beugré’s Prophétique , a 40-minute durational piece in which two performers (from a group of six) will read different excerpts from foundational texts for Diop and Beugré as a call and response. Listening to the words of Saidiya Hartman, Gayl Jones, Lucille Clifton, June Jordan, Toni Morrison, and others is a much-needed reprieve for the hustle and bustle of this week in Paris.", "links": [{"text": "Simone Leigh", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/t/simone-leigh/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "To learn more about Geste de Consolation , ARTnews spoke with Diop via a translator."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This interview has been lightly edited."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "ARTnews: How did the commissions for Fragments for Venus and then Geste de Consolation come together? Had you met Miuccia Prada prior to the invitation?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Alice Diop: I had no relationship with Miuccia Prada before I received an invitation from Verde Visconti to propose a project for the “Women’s Tales” series, and so that was Fragments for Venus . I met Mrs. Prada when Fragments was shown in Venice, and a few months ago, she offered me—to my great surprise—to be the invited artist for the public commission that Miu Miu has done for the last years during Art Basel Paris. I was stunned, but I decided to trust the intuition of this woman whom I greatly admire. I was glad that I did so because it really took me someplace different than I’ve been with the work that I’ve done in the past. With this project, I decided to stay true to the research that has inhabited me, haunted me, and that I have given shape to in Fragments . This research has to do with the questions that arise for me from the representation of Black women in art history, and I think this exhibition is a prolongation, a culmination, and perhaps the end of my research into these questions. It was really beautiful for me to be able to put in dialogue very specific objects that I chose for the exhibition and this venue."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/MMWT__30_ALICE_DIOP_PH.-BRIGITTE-LACOMBE-1.jpg?w=400", "alt": "Portrait of Alice Diop.", "caption": "Alice Diop. Photo Brigitte Lacombe", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Speaking about the representation of Black women in art history and in visual culture more generally, can you talk about the use of ethnographic films of African women in the short film, [Sans titres] , that you made for Geste de Consolation ?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I come from a background that is largely in ethnographic film or related to ethnographic film and anthropology. At university, I studied anthropology and history, and that’s what led me to cinema. The images that we see at the beginning of my video installation are ones that were found by a film archivist that I hired to look for them in the preparation for my next feature film, which is going to be an adaptation of Michel Leiris’s Phantom Africa , a text which is really the foundation of French anthropology and contemporary anthropology. It also reveals the extent to which this this dawning discipline in the 1930s was related to colonial domination and how anthropology and anthropological studies were the expression of a will to capture the other. So, this brilliant archivist who worked with me found these images from French, German, and Italian anthropological expeditions. [Sans titres] also includes excerpts from the [project funded] by Albert Kahn [ The Archives of the Planet ] to early Lumière films. There are also some private archival images, and some films from the 1930s, like Voyage au Congo (Voyage to the Congo). And so, what it really provides is a panorama of these types of images from the beginning of the 20th century to the middle of the 20th century, and I think that they reveal a collective imagination of the other. My gaze as a filmmaker has been developed against them. The way these images show and stage Black women tells me how I’ve been constructed and reveal how I became a filmmaker, to a large degree, to clean and heal myself."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Then, toward the end of the video installation, you have what I call images of consolation. These are images of care, and they include a variety of sources such as Ousmane Sembène’s La Noire de… [1966], a film by Sarah Maldoror called Sambizanga [1972]. There are some more recent images like from a film by Rosine Mbakam, Les prières de Delphine (Delphine’s Prayers) [2021]. There are images from a Chris Marker film, which are more ambiguous, and then you have images from Pedro Costa’s film Vitalina Varela [2019]. article_text:
For a few days this week, filmmaker Alice Diop has created a space for healing. For this year’s Miu Miu commission during Art Basel Paris, she has transformed the Place d’Iéna into a large-scale installation title Geste de Consolation (Gesture of Consolation).

The journey begins with Zanele Muholi’s Bona, Charlottesville, Virginia (2015), from the “Somnyama Ngonyama (Hail the Dark Lioness)” series. In the black-and-white photograph, we see the artist looking at themself in a mirror, but her face is only visible through their reflection. Beyond this is a new film by Diop, title [Sans titres] , which begins with excerpts from ethnographic films of African women, depicted as the other, and ending with shots that show empowered Black women.

Further along is “Chambre à soi” (Living Room and Library), which Diop describes as a “living room for a thinking Black woman—a space of pause, learning and encounter. Libraries have long been quietly radical spaces of Black political imagination.” In a space modeled after Diop’s own office, with rugs inspired by the visual motifs of Gee’s Bend quilter Mary Lee Bendolph, visitors can take time to read through books by Christina Sharpe, Virginia Woolf, and Jean Genet and peruse monographs on Otobong Nkanga, Deana Lawson, Henry Taylor, Chantal Akerman, Mona Hatoum, Jacqueline de Jong, Marcel Duchamp, and more.

Between the “Chambre à soi” and Simone Leigh ’s towering 2020–21 sculpture Sentinel (Mami Wata) , which concludes the journey, is a performance space, whose offerings will alternate between an embodied performance Angel Bat Dawid and the Sistazz of the Nitty Gritty and Nadia Beugré’s Prophétique , a 40-minute durational piece in which two performers (from a group of six) will read different excerpts from foundational texts for Diop and Beugré as a call and response. Listening to the words of Saidiya Hartman, Gayl Jones, Lucille Clifton, June Jordan, Toni Morrison, and others is a much-needed reprieve for the hustle and bustle of this week in Paris.

To learn more about Geste de Consolation , ARTnews spoke with Diop via a translator.

This interview has been lightly edited.

ARTnews: How did the commissions for Fragments for Venus and then Geste de Consolation come together? Had you met Miuccia Prada prior to the invitation?

Alice Diop: I had no relationship with Miuccia Prada before I received an invitation from Verde Visconti to propose a project for the “Women’s Tales” series, and so that was Fragments for Venus . I met Mrs. Prada when Fragments was shown in Venice, and a few months ago, she offered me—to my great surprise—to be the invited artist for the public commission that Miu Miu has done for the last years during Art Basel Paris. I was stunned, but I decided to trust the intuition of this woman whom I greatly admire. I was glad that I did so because it really took me someplace different than I’ve been with the work that I’ve done in the past. With this project, I decided to stay true to the research that has inhabited me, haunted me, and that I have given shape to in Fragments . This research has to do with the questions that arise for me from the representation of Black women in art history, and I think this exhibition is a prolongation, a culmination, and perhaps the end of my research into these questions. It was really beautiful for me to be able to put in dialogue very specific objects that I chose for the exhibition and this venue.

Speaking about the representation of Black women in art history and in visual culture more generally, can you talk about the use of ethnographic films of African women in the short film, [Sans titres] , that you made for Geste de Consolation ?

I come from a background that is largely in ethnographic film or related to ethnographic film and anthropology. At university, I studied anthropology and history, and that’s what led me to cinema. The images that we see at the beginning of my video installation are ones that were found by a film archivist that I hired to look for them in the preparation for my next feature film, which is going to be an adaptation of Michel Leiris’s Phantom Africa , a text which is really the foundation of French anthropology and contemporary anthropology. It also reveals the extent to which this this dawning discipline in the 1930s was related to colonial domination and how anthropology and anthropological studies were the expression of a will to capture the other. So, this brilliant archivist who worked with me found these images from French, German, and Italian anthropological expeditions. [Sans titres] also includes excerpts from the [project funded] by Albert Kahn [ The Archives of the Planet ] to early Lumière films. There are also some private archival images, and some films from the 1930s, like Voyage au Congo (Voyage to the Congo). And so, what it really provides is a panorama of these types of images from the beginning of the 20th century to the middle of the 20th century, and I think that they reveal a collective imagination of the other. My gaze as a filmmaker has been developed against them. The way these images show and stage Black women tells me how I’ve been constructed and reveal how I became a filmmaker, to a large degree, to clean and heal myself.

Then, toward the end of the video installation, you have what I call images of consolation. These are images of care, and they include a variety of sources such as Ousmane Sembène’s La Noire de… [1966], a film by Sarah Maldoror called Sambizanga [1972]. There are some more recent images like from a film by Rosine Mbakam, Les prières de Delphine (Delphine’s Prayers) [2021]. There are images from a Chris Marker film, which are more ambiguous, and then you have images from Pedro Costa’s film Vitalina Varela [2019]. These are all appearances of Black women on film who are shown with respect and dignity—images that helped me to heal and helped me to make more precise my own gaze as a filmmaker.

This reminds me of the second half of Fragments for Venus , where you focus on different Black women in Brooklyn. Do you see that part of the film as a form of healing that also adds to the visual archive of the representation of Black women?

Yes, absolutely. The pleasure I took in in doing this, and my primary intention in looking at these women, was looking at them the way I would have liked to be looked at when I was developing my gaze as a filmmaker.

In both Fragments for Venus and your feature film Saint Omer , you use music minimally but precisely. In [Sans Titre] , there’s music throughout the film. Why did you choose to approach the film’s score this way?

This is the first time I worked with a composer and had someone compose original music for one of my projects. It was really a tremendous pleasure that will certainly inspire me for my future films. I worked with Angel Bat Dawid and Naima Nefertari, whose album Journey to Nabta Playa really haunted the writing of my next feature film. I had used a piece from that album in early versions of the edit of this installation, and I felt that I wanted to do something more organic.

I think it was the right instinct to have Angel and Naima come in and work on this film because there was a very tricky question about how to use these images, including how to expose Black women to these images. I didn’t want to show them this violence again in a way that was going to hurt them. This was a very tricky question, and I found that the only way to do it was actually for music to give us the point of view on how I wanted these images to be looked at. The resulting music is [a recording of] Black women looking at these images, crying, praying, consoling, avenging—and that’s really what happened. Naima and Angel came to the studio with me. We set up the screens. The three of us watched the images together. We cried, and then they composed in a very organic way to the image. It was like a live film concert—they performed live to these archival images. It was a tremendously powerful experience. Then the next day, I edited the music to the image, but [there was] very little editing, because, again, it was so organic. The relationship between the voice, the crying, the calling out of Angel and her clarinet and Naima’s piano—it was so accurate. It made me realize that this was actually the only voiceover possible, and it was the only way to confront viewers with these images.

How did you approach the architecture of the Place d’Iéna for the commission, and how does that relate to the Zanele Muholi and Simone Leigh works, as well as the performance program?

Well, it’s like a trajectory or a path. What is important is that there was precise attention devoted to each object that’s exhibited. At the same time, I wanted to allow visitors freedom to move from one space to another. It really is a path from the photo to the sculpture. I can’t predict what visitors are going to experience because it’s very personal. But the idea is that it’s a kind of narrative path toward care, toward healing. The relationship between each of these objects that appear along a very considered trajectory is precise. We start with Zanele’s photo, which I think of as the point of view that I’d like people to have toward the images, and then the installation space with the video is the space of violence and raises the need for consolation. Then we have the performance space where these women just come out of the frame and are totally themselves. They claim the right to be themselves, and suddenly we have them there in all their beauty and all their power.

‘Clayface’ on track for profitable outcome

Warner Bros’ DC Studios is bouncing back from its Supergirl disappointment with the opening numbers for Clayface : an estimated $24.0m in North America and $19.0m across international markets.

While the $43m opening is lower that Supergirl ’s $67m worldwide debut in June, the new film looks on a steady trajectory to profitability given a fiscally responsible production budget reported at $44m. Supergirl , which grossed $126.5m lifetime in cinemas, had a production budget above $170m – leaving plenty of red ink on the balance sheet when revenue shares with cinemas and marketing costs are factored in.

Among international markets, Clayface scored best in UK/Ireland, with an estimated $2.6m, almost double second-placed Mexico ($1.4m). Next come Australia ($1.3m), France ($1.2m), Brazil ($879,000), Italy ($873,000) and Spain ($721,000). In Brazil, the film faced the distraction of the presidential runoff election on Sunday.

Germany, the ninth-biggest opener with an estimated $593,000, is traditionally a weaker territory for DC Studios, relative to the other large European countries. In 2025, Germany was well behind the pace on DC hit Superman , grossing $6.5m lifetime – which compared to $37.9m in UK/Ireland and $13.2m in France.

Still to open Clayface are Poland, Japan and Vietnam, which all welcome the film this coming weekend.

Clayface is directed by James Watkins ( Speak No Evil ) from a screenplay by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini. Tom Rhys Harries and Naomi Ackie lead the cast, with David Dencik, Max Minghella and Eddie Marsan.

‘Wildwood’ makes solid start

Animation house Laika will be hoping for sustained success for its new stop-motion film Wildwood after opening numbers that are a big improvement on 2019’s Missing Link , albeit in a similar ballpark to 2016’s Kubo And The Two Strings .

Wildwood has debuted with an estimated $11.8m in North America (via Fathom Entertainment) and $2.9m across 10 early international markets, yielding an opening salvo of $14.7m. UK/Ireland, via Black Bear, looks set to deliver close to half of the international opening number (around $1.4m). Australia comes next with an estimated $391,000, followed by Italy ($249,000) and Spain ($183,000).

Missing Link launched with $5.9m in North America on its way to a weak $26.6m worldwide lifetime total. Kubo And The Two Strings began with $12.6m in North America, and reached $76.3m worldwide lifetime. (Comparisons in this report are not adjusted for inflation.)

Given the buzz on Wildwood and its perceived status as an Oscar frontrunner, Laika must be hoping to achieve a higher box office bar with its new film. However, providing a challenge is the certification: PG-13 in the US and 12A in the UK, after the five previous Laika films were all rated PG in both markets. Can the loss of families with younger children be compensated by stronger teen and adult audiences?

Providing a target for Wildwood are Laika’s Boxtrolls and ParaNorman , two films that reached similar worldwide lifetime totals – respectively $108.3m and $107.4m in 2014 and 2012, according to available data. In 2010, Coraline grossed $127.0m worldwide, and re-releases take that number up to $188.8m – Laika’s biggest success to date.

The expansive Wildwood , which is based on the 2011 novel by Colin Melloy and Carson Ellis, has a production budget reported at $100m. Laika CEO Travis Knight ( Kubo And The Two Strings ) directs. The global rollout is ongoing, and stretches into January 2027.

‘You Can See Everything’ rises to second place at global box office

Source: A24

‘You Can See Everything’

Hefty falls for other titles in the market such as Street Fighter , plus the relative lack of powerful new releases, have helped You Can See Everything rise from last weekend’s seventh place in the worldwide ranking to second place this time around. This is despite currently playing in just a single market: North America.

The A24 documentary saw box office rise by 25% on an expanded footprint of cinemas. Estimated second-weekend takings of $19.5m take that total after 10 days to $45.1m.

You Can See Everything is directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, and the film has grossed in 10 days almost as much as Oppenheim’s other current film, scripted drama Primetime , has achieved after five weeks ($46.5m).

Both films will be profitable: Primetime has a production budget reported at $14.5m and You Can See Everything at $7m.

Global rollout for the documentary will follow. The UK/Ireland release is set for November 20 via A24.

Worldwide total for the Paramount Pictures/ Legendary Pictures/ Capcom film after two weekends is $79.6m.

Sony’s Resident Evil is holding better, especially in international markets where the drop was 41% in its sixth weekend of play. Worldwide total is now $384.5m on the Zach Cregger film from TriStar Pictures, Constantin Film and Davis Films, buoyed by $65.0m so far in China, and setting a Resident Evil franchise record globally.

Tamil-language action comedy Jailer 2 and US studio titles Verity , Other Mommy , Heart Of The Beast and Whalefall make up the bottom half of the worldwide weekend top 10. Sliding out of the chart to make way for Clayface and Wildwood are Universal’s Sense And Sensibility and Chinese crime drama Traces Of Justice .

article_text:
In May, Theaster Gates set a precedent for restitution by transferring ownership of a stoneware vessel by David Drake , an enslaved ceramist widely known as “Dave the Potter,” to his descendants. The family estimates that some 200 of Drake’s surviving works remain in the possession of museums and collectors, though a growing number of institutions are agreeing to its request: return Drake’s work to his family, and we’ll keep it on view and accessible to the public.

The Hampton University Museum, in Virginia, offers a model of how such a deal works. The institution announced Tuesday that it will accept a loan of the vessel returned by Gates. Beginning Wednesday October 21, the work will go on view through May 2027. Drake’s piece will be in good company: the Hampton University Museum’s collection includes works by Henry O. Tanner, one of the first African American painters to earn international renown, known for his dignified depictions of Black subjects and biblical scenes; and Thomas Day, a master cabinetmaker and free man of color from North Carolina.

“It is indeed an honor to showcase this historic pottery,” Hampton University museum director Dr. Vanessa Thaxton-Ward, said in a statement, expressing “great thanks to the Drake family descendants.”

David Drake’s profile has risen dramatically within the mainstream art world over the past decade, buoyed by his biography and skill. He was born into enslavement in Edgefield District, South Carolina, bound by laws that forbade Black literacy. Defiantly, he made some 40,000 jars in bondage, inscribing many with his name and even with poems of his own devising. ARTnews named Drake’s Storage Jar , from 1857, the greatest artwork about the United States of America. (One side of the pot reads: “When you fill this Jar with pork or beef / Scot will be there; to get a peace, — / Dave.”)

In 2021, Drake set the world auction record for American pottery when his 25-gallon stoneware jar sold for $1.56 million at Crocker Farm. The following year, his art drew institutional attention with “Hear Me Now: The Black Potters of Old Edgefield, South Carolina,” which debuted at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York before traveling to Boston, Atlanta, and Ann Arbor, Michigan. After this show, Drake’s descendants began in earnest their mission to reclaim ownership of the art.

Since 2025, the family has reportedly reached agreements of what it describes as “ethical restitution” with five museums and two collectors, including the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts; the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston; the Georgia Museum of Art, in Athens; the Telfair Museums, in Savannah, Georgia; and the Milwaukee Art Museum. Each institution contacted is offered the choice to repurchase or deaccession its jar.

“When I look at Dave’s pottery, I think about the conditions he was living in and the courage it took for him to write his name and poetry into the clay. Our ancestor left something for his family to find—a voice, a connection, a way to know him,” said Yaba Baker, David Drake’s fourth-great-grandson, in a statement, thanking Theaster Gates for his part.

Baker added, “Loaning this jar to Hampton University Museum is a full-circle moment for me. I attended Hampton, and it literally changed my life! Playing a role in my alma mater being the first HBCU to show a Drake jar fills me with joy and pride.”

The artist’s exhibition in London lets us feel what trusting historical and colonial documentary has always cost

Three drawings of a photographer cast eye and camera across Alma Pearl. In the case of Celestino (RGB) (all works 2026) the exhibition text identifies its central character as the protagonist of Roberto Rossellini’s La Macchina Ammazzacattivi (The Machine to Kill Bad People, 1952), versioned in crisp red, green and blue. In the film, Celestino wields the gift of a magic camera that functions as a gun, killing only ‘bad people’ – one reference among the many Lyndon Barrois Jr. pulls across the exhibition, from the mining of National Geographic magazines to citations across cinematic history. The coolly rendered photographer means little until supplied with its murderous backstory, at which Celestino’s blank affect curdles into something threatening. In multiple works, appropriated National Geographic advertisements are central: in Aim High , cuttings sit on raw linen bordered by a painted yellow edge (mimicking the magazine’s iconic cover); images of home-computer software and a NASA Space Shuttle stage capitalist aspirations and futurity, offset by a patinaed solvent-transfer of a child in a classroom. Elsewhere, rulers, colour charts and archaeological and surveying equipment recur: instruments that lent documentation its claim to objectivity are placed against advertisements that perpetuate ideas over facts, exposing these systems as arbitrary.

A triptych of oil paintings, Unrest (RGB) , reproduces a sign from Cyril Schäublin’s film Unrest (2022), set in a Swiss watch factory, another reference revealed by the extensive exhibition text. In muddy shades of red, green and blue is the decree, ‘Soyez bref, vos minutes sont aussi précieuses que les nôtres’ (be brief, your time is as precious as ours). Barrois Jr. frames his concerns with authority and verification by abstracting the sign from its source. However, like the Celestino drawings, the piece asks a fluency of the viewer to fully participate in the show’s network of references. This demand feels intentional: an exhibition interrogating ‘who’ gets to classify and document can hardly avoid implicating its own reliance on specialist knowledge. The artist’s own erudition becomes another perpetuating system asking to be taken on faith.

Source Material (Promise) holds a series of National Geographic magazines, heavily thumbed, inside a grey archival box, atop a cerulean film canister caressed by a limp conservation glove. Its theatrical staging imbues the sculpture with an uncanny tang: the yet-to-be-altered objects let us metabolise the idea that the artist will continue to extract from this material, as the magazine’s original photographers once extracted from the globe. But where the wall-based works reframe their source material more fully, the sculptural readymade doesn’t need this archival cosplay. Appraised away from the orientation of the wall, the effectiveness of these objects and Barrois Jr.’s particular dialectic of assembling disparate referents falls away, exposing how much of the associative work is done for the viewer by the conventions of display. In contrast, To save endangered shines in its austerity, a National Geographic DSLR cameras advertisement, held behind a plexiglass enclosure protruding from a nondescript suggestion box. Alluring in its simple fusion of disparities, it is indexical: the advertisement protruding from an actual suggestion box, physical systems under scrutiny, not the image of them. This directness lets us feel what trusting historical and colonial documentary has always cost, without the explanatory apparatus the show leans on elsewhere.

Lyndon Barrois Jr.: Desert of Promise is on view at Alma Pearl, London, 10 September – 24 October

The MIT Professors Bedazzling Security Cameras to Highlight Campus Surveillance

The intervention is responding to the university’s recent $3 million investment in more than 500 new AI-integrated campus surveillance cameras.

Tenured faculty members at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) are decorating the university's surveillance cameras with googly eyes, rhinestones, and glitzy decorations to protest its investment in what they call "Big Brother technology."

Faculty members Catherine D'Ignazio, Marah Gubar, Tanalís Padilla, Dwai Banerjee, and Karrie Karahalios began decorating the cameras in August, four months after the student newspaper, The Tech , reported that MIT would be spending over $3 million on more than 500 surveillance cameras from 2025 to 2026. According to the report, the cameras can be activated to identify faces and objects with AI, and are stationed in exterior locations and academic facilities, among other high-traffic areas around campus.

"We have these little buckets of gems and tinsel, and create these little Gumby-type creatures with googly eyes," D'Ignazio told Hyperallergic in a phone interview. None of the adornments interfere with the camera function, but are intended to remind passersby that they are under surveillance.

In a faculty newsletter announcing the deliberately unwieldy project name, "The Initiative to Beautify the AI-capable Surveillance Benevolently Installed by our Administrator Overseers and the MIT Corporation In Collaboration with Big Brother Tech Companies," the faculty members said that the campus had been transformed into an "AI-capable Panopticon."

"Many of us would not feel safer with cameras on all around us, especially not ones with AI," Gubar told Hyperallergic over the phone. While the university established a faculty advisory committee to determine whether the cameras should utilize AI technology, many eligible members were barred from participating, as first reported by local outlet Cambridge Day .

"They knew where we were coming from and what our viewpoint on the committee would be," D'Ignazio added. "Our viewpoint isn't just a matter of opinion. It's grounded in scholarly expertise. I've worked on how data, surveillance, and technology particularly affects women and marginalized groups."

An MIT spokesperson told Hyperallergic that the new cameras are "intended to close gaps in MIT’s existing security camera coverage."

Faculty took inspiration from artist and MIT alumnus Jill Magid , who rhinestoned CCTV cameras at Amsterdam's police headquarters in 2002.

"I wanted to question the visible and invisible parts of surveillance," Magid told Hyperallergic . After Amsterdam police initially turned down the artist's request to bedazzle the cameras, Magid created her own temporary fictitious company, System Azure Security Ornamentation, and successfully got herself a paid job. She advertised her business on silk screen posters that read "Big Brother in Drag," and when the larger police system shut down her enterprise, she distributed flyers urging, "Bring Back the Glam."

Faculty printed out several of Magid's posters and distributed them to students, faculty, and staff, many of whom have joined in on the seven decoration sessions so far.

While MIT Police usually only intervene by removing the decorations after the sessions, Gubar allegedly had to give her name to a suspicious officer on one occasion.

"I wasn't going to let a student or staff member give their name," said Gubar, who clarified that her tenured status protects her from severe administrative pushback.

The professor has noticed that most other participants, especially students, are hesitant to speak out about the surveillance cameras or disclose their names for fear of retaliation, an anxiety confirmed by other universities' tactics and actions. During the 2023-4 academic year, Columbia University's surveillance cameras helped administrators identify and punish pro-Palestine student protesters. In May 2026, a pro-Palestine student filed a federal lawsuit against the University of Michigan for surveilling and harassing him over his advocacy.

"The goal should be for all of us to be able to protest against surveillance, whether that be students or staff," Gubar added. "It shouldn't just be a privilege for tenured faculty."

article_text:
As Jimmy Fallon gears up for Halloween, he and his latest talk show guest nailed their take on You Can See Everything .

On Wednesday’s episode of The Tonight Show , the 6x Emmy-winning host channeled his inner Nathan Fielder to grill Jamie Lee Curtis as Elizabeth Holmes during the NBC talk show’s cold open.

“Be honest, do you really want to be on the show tonight,” asked Fallon, mimicking Fielder’s line of questioning in the much meme-ified teaser , as Curtis responded in her most convincing Holmes voice, “Of course I do. I love talking to you.”

The late-night parody of You Can See Everything comes as the Lance Oppenheim-helmed doc surpasses $45M worldwide in A24’s slow-burn expanding release, building buzz for its acclaimed portrait of the incarcerated Theranos founder.

article_text:
Through the iconography of opera and martial arts to a burst dam, the artist’s video and photoworks interrogate the nature of human displacement

Chen Qiulin grew up in what’s now Wanzhou, a small county in Chongqing in southwestern China. Her hometown fell directly in the path of the Three Gorges Dam, the completion of which, in 2003, when the artist was beginning her career, submerged close to half of it.

This profound change prompted Chen to interrogate the nature of human displacement: when everything that anchors memory has vanished, where does the past reside? In Heartland the artist reveals a particular sensitivity to the concept of home, the exhibition showcasing a selection of the artist’s better-known works spanning more than two decades of Chen’s practice.

In Farewell Poem (2002), a single-channel videowork filmed at a demolition site in her hometown before it was submerged, she dresses as Consort Yu, wife of the third-century BCE warlord Xiang Yu, and acts out passages from the classic Chinese opera Farewell My Concubine (1918), channelling her childhood martial arts and dance lessons undertaken in a neighbourhood surrounded by opera performers. The visual contrast between her brightly coloured attire and the monochromatic ruins echo the disparity between ideal and reality, evoking a poignant sense of absurdity while capturing the dissonance felt by individuals confronting traumatic change.

The Three Gorges Dam project precipitated migration on a vast scale, forcing more than 260,000 residents of Wanzhou to relocate within Chongqing. Turning her lens towards this uprooted population, Chen created the videowork The Garden (2007), in which she hired a group of Chongqing’s bangbang men, the city’s once-ubiquitous porters, and instructed these workers to carry oversize, trophylike bouquets of artificial peonies and wander aimlessly through the urban landscape to the distorted soundtrack of Wahaha (1956), a patriotic Chinese children’s song. In Chinese culture, peonies traditionally signify prosperity and belonging. As the title implies, the workers form a mobile garden, yet the flowers are fake – symbols of rootedness abstracted and drifting in the hands of manual labourers who have lost their homes.

While Chen’s earlier works drew mainly from personal experience, the process of recognising, understanding and reconciling with change is a collective phenomenon; over the past 40 years, rapid urbanisation has taken place across all of China. In the Another Day series (2014–16), she examines communities in rural Guizhou, in which elderly unmarried women choose to remain in their ancestral homes in impoverished villages while the rest of their families move to larger cities for work or study. Chen asks how we come to terms with ourselves and our place in an ever-shifting world: for local visitors at Pingshan Art Museum, such a question hits close to home. Set within a newly developing district of Shenzhen defined by raw construction sites and transient communities, the exhibition venue mirrors the very societal shifts Chen interrogates. Here, displacement is largely voluntary – driven by young people leaving their hometowns for megacity opportunities – yet the psychic weight of uprootedness lingers all the same.

Chen Qiulin: Heartland at Pingshan Art Museum, Shenzhen, 30 May – 30 August

article_text:
Judi Dench , who played Old Deuteronomy in Tom Hooper’s “ Cats ,” is reflecting on the universally panned film in her forthcoming memoir, “Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It?”

Released in 2019, the film adapted Andrew Lloyd Webber’s hugely successful musical of the same name. But despite its stacked cast — which also included James Corden, Idris Elba, Taylor Swift and others among Dench — the film was considered a critical and commercial failure.

Related Stories

'Coven Academy' Renewed for Season 2 at Disney

“Oh God, I can’t bear it – and [Lloyd Webber] had waited so long for it to be made,” she wrote. “What a waste of all that goodwill and talent. I understand the critics were rather hostile to the film. I never saw the final cut so I can’t judge. All I’ll say is nobody sets out to give a poor performance or make a bad film. You do your best, offer something up and hope that people will get on board and join the party.” (Dench was nominated for a Razzie award for her performance in the film.)

She also added, “It’s a miracle that anything is ever made – films, plays, TV – let alone turn out to be a success, because there are so many moving parts,” speaking about the industry at large.

“Sometimes things just don’t work out: the timing’s wrong, the cast don’t gel, the elements don’t coalesce,” she wrote. “But people’s intentions are mostly honorable. There were no villains in the making of Cats. And if something isn’t a success, then there are always things you can say you’ve learnt.”

“Is It Too Late to Make a Run For It?” hits shelves Nov. 3.

article_text:
È morto Mario Pieroni , gallerista, collezionista e promotore culturale che dagli anni Settanta ha attraversato alcune delle esperienze più significative dell’arte contemporanea italiana. Aveva 88 anni.

La sua storia professionale si è sviluppata tra Pescara e Roma, attraverso la Galleria Pieroni e successivamente con progetti come Zerynthia, RAM – radioartemobile e No Man’s Land Foundation, sempre costruiti attorno al rapporto diretto con gli artisti e a un’idea dell’arte come spazio di ricerca e di relazione.

«Io sono un gallerista. Il gallerista esprime sempre una sua visione, un suo pensiero, non segue l’ottica del mercato», aveva spiegato in un’intervista del 2015, marcando una distinzione che avrebbe accompagnato tutto il suo percorso: quella tra il lavoro culturale del gallerista e quello strettamente commerciale del mercante.

Dall’Abruzzo alla Galleria Pieroni

Il percorso di Pieroni nell’arte prende forma a Pescara all’inizio degli anni Settanta. Proveniva da una famiglia attiva nel settore dell’arredamento e dell’antiquariato e nel 1970 avviò Il mondo delle idee , progetto dedicato alla produzione di oggetti e multipli d’artista che coinvolse figure come Getulio Alviani , Mario Ceroli e, attraverso riedizioni di arredi storici, Giacomo Balla .

Nel 1975 nacque quindi la Galleria Pieroni negli spazi del Bagno Borbonico di Pescara, antiche prigioni trasformate in luogo espositivo. Le prime esperienze chiarirono subito la direzione della ricerca: il rapporto con Luciano Fabro , Mario Merz , Jannis Kounellis , Vettor Pisani , Ettore Spalletti e Gino De Dominicis costruì una rete fondata più sulla frequentazione e sul confronto che sulla tradizionale idea di “scuderia” di una galleria.

Nel 1977 l’incontro con Dora Stiefelmeier aprì una nuova fase personale e professionale. Due anni più tardi i due trasferirono l’attività a Roma: nel gennaio 1979 la Galleria Pieroni inaugurò in via Panisperna con una collettiva di De Dominicis, Kounellis e Spalletti. Tra il 1979 e il 1992 la sede romana ospitò decine di esposizioni e divenne uno dei luoghi di riferimento per le ricerche concettuali, ambientali e post-minimali della capitale.

Merz, Kounellis e le nuove ricerche degli anni Ottanta

La storia della Galleria Pieroni incrocia alcuni dei principali protagonisti dell’Arte Povera e della ricerca concettuale. Nel suo programma passarono artisti come Alighiero Boetti , Luciano Fabro , Jannis Kounellis , Mario Merz , Giulio Paolini , Michelangelo Pistoletto , Emilio Prini ed Ettore Spalletti, insieme a figure indipendenti come Carla Accardi , Meret Oppenheim e Gerhard Richter .

Negli anni Ottanta la galleria si aprì inoltre a una nuova generazione e alla scena internazionale, presentando artisti come Marco Bagnoli , Bizhan Bassiri , Franz West , Günther Förg , Bertrand Lavier e Jan Vercruysse . Il filo conduttore era un’idea della galleria come luogo di produzione culturale e di sperimentazione, per accompagnare il lavoro degli artisti senza ridurlo alle sole logiche del mercato.

Questa impostazione sarebbe stata ricostruita nel 2025 al MAXXI con In viaggio per l’arte. La Galleria Pieroni 1975-1992 , mostra dedicata all’archivio della galleria e curata da Stefano Chiodi . L’esposizione restituiva la storia di uno spazio che, tra Pescara e Roma, aveva seguito quasi due decenni di trasformazioni dell’arte contemporanea attraverso mostre, incontri, documenti e relazioni personali.

Zerynthia e l’arte oltre la galleria

Nel 1992 Pieroni e Stiefelmeier decisero di chiudere la galleria. Non fu un allontanamento dall’arte ma un cambiamento di struttura. Come avrebbero raccontato anni dopo, la crescente centralità delle dinamiche commerciali li portò a cercare modalità differenti di lavoro, capaci di sostenere progetti più complessi e meno vincolati al modello tradizionale della galleria.

Nacque così Zerynthia – Associazione per l’Arte Contemporanea , il cui nome, scelto dal figlio poeta Daniele Pieroni, deriva da una farfalla e richiama l’idea della metamorfosi. Il progetto estese il lavoro di Pieroni a interventi, mostre e collaborazioni in contesti differenti, mantenendo al centro il dialogo con gli artisti.

A questa esperienza si sarebbe affiancata RAM – radioartemobile , piattaforma dedicata al rapporto tra arte contemporanea e suono, e successivamente No Man’s Land Foundation a Loreto Aprutino, progetto nato dall’incontro con Yona Friedman e Jean-Baptiste Decavèle e pensato come luogo aperto di sperimentazione tra arte, territorio e ricerca. Ancora nell’ottobre 2026 Mario Pieroni era indicato tra i protagonisti delle attività della fondazione. A proposito della fondazione, aveva raccontato a exibart in questa intervista : «No Man’s Land riguarda tutti. No Man’s Land è terra di tutti, è per tutti e richiede il coinvolgimento di tutti. Rappresenta un’idea di libertà a cui ognuno di noi anela nella propria vita. Quindi, è nato questo progetto che ospita anche lavori di grandi artisti che di volta in volta si sono aggiunti. Ma l’idea parte da Yona Friedman. È stato lui a chiamarlo No Man’s Land. Le prime installazioni sono sue insieme a Jean-Baptiste Decavèle. Yona ha sempre detto “Io sono un architetto, non un artista, organizzo lo spazio come un luogo per tutti”».

Visualizza questo post su Instagram Un post condiviso da Zerynthia and RAM (@zerynthia_contemporaryart)

Una collezione costruita attraverso le relazioni

Anche la collezione sviluppata con Dora Stiefelmeier riflette questo metodo. Più che attraverso una strategia sistematica di acquisizione, si è formata nel corso dei decenni come conseguenza di rapporti personali, collaborazioni e affinità con gli artisti.

Nel 2026 una selezione della raccolta è stata presentata a Villa Pacchiani, a Santa Croce sull’Arno, nella mostra Opere dalla Collezione Pieroni – Stiefelmeier . Il progetto, curato da Alessandro Cocchieri , riuniva lavori di Carla Accardi, Vito Acconci, Marco Bagnoli, Mirosław Bałka, Bizhan Bassiri, Gianfranco Baruchello, Jimmie Durham, Cristina Iglesias, Jannis Kounellis, Joseph Kosuth, Sol LeWitt, Luigi Ontani, Giulio Paolini, Remo Salvadori ed Ettore Spalletti, tra gli altri.

Pochi mesi prima, Mario Pieroni aveva inoltre donato, insieme a Michelangelo Pistoletto , due opere dell’artista alla Fondazione Pescarabruzzo, destinate al percorso permanente del MicHub di Pescara: un ulteriore segno del rapporto mai interrotto con l’Abruzzo e con una storia iniziata proprio lì oltre cinquant’anni fa.

Con Mario Pieroni scompare così una figura che ha attraversato il sistema dell’arte assumendo ruoli differenti ma mantenendo costante una convinzione: che il valore del lavoro del gallerista risieda prima di tutto nella capacità di riconoscere, accompagnare e mettere in relazione le ricerche degli artisti.

article_text:
独特な佇まいとキレのあるセリフで、「豊臣兄弟！」屈指の人気キャラクターとなった徳川家康。松下洸平さん演じる家康公が登場するとファンが盛り上がり、 SNS の反響が多くなります。第 41 回「家康の野望」では、とうとう家康が豊臣家に臣従を誓いました。存在感のある役をどのような思いで演じられているのか、松下さんにお話を伺いました。（場面写真は NHK 提供）

家康を“かわいいな”と思った

――第 41 回で秀長（仲野太賀さん）と対峙するシーンでは、どんな点を意識されましたか？

松下さん ：家康には作戦があったので、序盤はじっくりと楽しむように会話を進めるのですが、中盤にかけて思いもよらぬ言葉が秀長から返ってきて動揺し、最終的に豊臣兄弟の熱意に押されてしまいます。そのグラデーションをしっかり作りたいと思いながら演じていました。太賀君とは事前に話し合いはしなかったのですが、太賀くんのお芝居に助けていただきながら、家康が余裕のある状態から少しずつ追い詰められていく過程を演じることができました。

――秀長とのやりとりで、特に印象に残った部分は？

松下さん ：「徳川殿が楽しいと思うことは何ですか」と聞かれたとき、「薬草集め」と答える部分が“かわいいな”と思いました（笑）。このセリフ、脚本家の八津弘幸さんはどんな風に言ってほしいのかなと悩みましたが、笑わそうと思って言うとおもしろくないので、ふざけず大きい声で言いました。太賀君の受けとめ方も最高でした。

家康は本当に臣従を誓ったのか？

――その後、大坂城で秀吉（池松壮亮さん）に臣従を誓うとき、月代姿で現れますが、家康にどんな思いがあったと解釈されていますか？

松下さん ：頭をそって月代にするのは、最大級の敬意だったのではないかと解釈しました。豊臣傘下に入る決意の表れだったと思いますし、監督もその決意が伝わるように演出してくださいました。

――今までの家康を見ると、本心から秀吉への臣従を誓っているのか、疑ってしまいます。

松下さん ：本心から誓っていると考えていただいていいと思います（笑）。ただ、これまでたくさん嘘をついてきたので、僕がどれだけ頭を下げても視聴者のみなさんに信じてもらえないかもという不安はあります（笑）。あの兄弟をリスペクトしたのは真実だと思いますが、豊臣の中には石川数正（迫田孝也さん）もいます。これからも自分に通じよ、と家康が数正に言う場面もあるので、豊臣の支配下にいながら、やはり家康なりの野望は消えたわけではないと思います。

憎めない存在でいてほしい

――豊臣兄弟の二人をどう捉えていますか。

松下さん ：今までの家康の人生には存在しなかったキャラクターだと思うので、どう戦うべきか、頭を悩ませたと思います。あの兄弟は魅力的で、どこまでもピュア。第 5 回で、藤吉郎（秀吉）に「熱意が人を動かし、勝敗を決する」と言いました。当時は、真逆のことを言ってやったと思っていましたが、最終的にはその言葉が自分に返ってきて、兄弟の熱意に家康が動かされるという展開が、おもしろいなと思いました。

――第 5 回のセリフが第 41 回に出てきたとき、どうお感じになりましたか。

松下さん ：なるほどと思いました。第 5 回を撮影しているとき、僕は現場にも慣れていなくて本当に緊張していました。馬に乗りながら、必死にセリフを言っていたのですが、まさか第 41 回で出てくるとは思っていなかったので、もっとかっこよく言えばよかったなと思いました ( 笑 ) 。

――第 34 回で描かれた、人質時代のエピソードも印象的でした。

松下さん ：幼少期の家康を演じさせていただけて、とても良かったです。「奪われる前に奪う」は第 41 回に続く大事なキーワードで、家康の考え方がしっかりと植え付けられたシーンでもあります。家康は飄々として腹の底が見えない人ですが、苦しい思いもたくさんしてきたので、ただのヒールではない、憎めない存在でいてほしいなと思いながら演じています。

役所広司さんの家康で学ぶ

――今まで、徳川家康についてはどんなイメージをお持ちでしたか？

松下さん ：クールでかっこいいイメージで、僕もそうなるのかと思っていたのですが、八津さんが脚本でコミカルに描いてくださって（笑）。そのおかげで、自分でも想像していなかったような家康になったと感じていますし、とても楽しかったです。

――家康を演じるにあたり、参考にした俳優さんはいらっしゃいますか？

松下さん ：役所広司さんが演じられた徳川家康を拝見して、時代劇におけるお芝居を勉強させていただきました。結果的には真似もできないですし到底及びませんが、役所さんのお芝居をとても尊敬しています。

迫田さんがいたから自然体でお芝居できた

――豊臣兄弟に対する本音を語る家康がコミカルですが、何か意識されていますか？

松下さん ：本当におもしろい人は、自分がおもしろいことに気づいていないと思っているので、僕はすごく真面目に演じました。数正との掛け合いでは、迫田さんの間の使い方が最高なので、お任せしていました。

――迫田さんとのコンビ、息が合っていますね。

松下さん ：迫田さんなくして、僕の家康はないと思います。どんな芝居も受け止めてくださる迫田さんがいたから、僕も自然体でお芝居できました。毎シーン、迫田さんに助けていただきました。

――数正とのシーンでお気に入りは？

松下さん ：第 41 回の、二人で酒を飲み交わすシーンです。迫田さんのオールアップのタイミングでもあったので、今までの 1 年間を思い出しながら、格別の敬意と感謝を込めて、かみしめるようにセリフを言いました。

今後の見どころは…

――家康が出てくると、 SNS の反響が多くなりますが、どう受け止めていますか？

松下さん ：やはり大河ドラマはすごいと思います。「家康さん」と声をかけられる機会が多く、夢中になって見てくださっているという実感があります。みなさんに、今回の家康が天下を取る姿を見たいと思っていただけるように、最後までこの奥深い役を追求していきたいと思います。

――第 41 回以降の家康は、どうなりますか？

松下さん ：今も日々悩みながら撮影しています。今後は、秀長とも交流を深めていくと思います。

――最後に、視聴者のみなさんにメッセージをお願いします。

松下さん ：撮影もラストスパートに入りましたが、最後まで気を抜かず、視聴者のみなさんに楽しんでもらえるような作品を作りたいと思っています。この先も涙と笑顔がたくさん詰まったドラマが生まれるので、一緒に最後まで駆け抜けていっていただければうれしいです。

松下洸平（まつした・こうへい） さん 1987年生まれ、東京都出身。俳優、シンガーソングライター。主な出演作は、映画『燃えよ剣』『遠い山なみの光』、ドラマ『最愛』『放課後カルテ』、連続テレビ小説『スカーレット』、大河ドラマ『光る君へ』など多数。エランドール賞新人賞、文化庁芸術祭新人賞、読売演劇大賞優秀男優賞、杉村春子賞を受賞。

article_text:
Released in October 2026 and unconnected to current events, the book GenZ published by La Belle Étoile* gathers 230 portraits of teenagers from Generation Z, photographed in the studio by photographer Stéphane Coutelle between 2022 and 2026.

A series born of the photographer’s personal experience, his teenage child’s declaration of non-binarity, which led him to want to discover and understand Generation Z with empathy, openness and generosity.

Four years of rich encounters, rendered with sensitivity and restraint.

The Project

This series came into being from an intensely formative personal experience: almost five years ago, Stéphane Coutelle’s daughter, then 14, came out to him as non-binary. As a portrait photographer, photography was naturally his way of grappling with his questions about this Generation Z that is pushing boundaries.

To meet and talk with Generation Z teenagers, the best way was to make their portraits. The first sitters spread the word on social media, connections were made, and sessions followed one another quickly. No casting: everyone who wants to pose is photographed. The only rule: be between 13 and 19, and come with others. The photographer is delighted to see that the panel quickly broadened to include all styles, all origins and all social backgrounds.

The session always unfolds the same way. Over a coffee or a glass of water, Stéphane Coutelle and his sitters get to know each other. The photographer explains the project to them and shows them the photos. The teenagers are always pleased to see all this diversity and happy that their singularity is being added to this mosaic. The photographer tells them that at the end of the session he will ask them about their dream, which now appears in the book. The shoot generally lasts half an hour, with no intervention from the photographer on the looks chosen by his sitters.

Stéphane Coutelle was surprised by the contrast between the peaceful, joyful encounters in his studio, and these teens’ kindness toward him, a “straight cis boomer,” on the one hand, and the passionate reactions the photos provoke in their parents’ generation on the other. The photographer’s ambition in this book is to bear witness to the richness of these roughly 250 encounters and, beyond that, to restore a societal bond and an intergenerational dialogue strained by incomprehension.

To see the full GenZ series:

https://www.stephanecoutelle.com/gen-z

The Website

Beyond the photos, Stéphane Coutelle wanted to give a voice to the teenagers he had photographed. After all, who better than they to speak about their generation?

The book is therefore accompanied by a website where 160 participants in the project answer ten questions. The questions and their answers appear on the site in random order.

Their answers? Just like them: deep, interesting, sometimes funny, always sincere.

Alongside the book: the website https://genz.coutelle.com/

The Photographer

A portrait photographer, Stéphane Coutelle has had a very varied career, always driven by the desire to reinvent himself and explore new territories.

In the 1980s, he made fashion photographs and celebrity portraits. In the 1990s, he became a painter, creating large, hypnotic portraits. He then returned to photography, building a fine career in advertising photography and beauty commercials.

In parallel, Stéphane Coutelle never stopped working on personal projects. He has published five books:

Me, Myself and I in 1995

Shoebox Studio in 2012

Insomnies in 2014

CARBONE in 2019

2020 in 2021

Since 2019, Stéphane Coutelle has taught portrait photography at the École des Gobelins in Paris.

He also works as an editor and art director of photo books (Stefan Rappo, Sofiya Loriashvili…), heading La Belle Étoile*, a publishing house and gallery in book form co-founded with his partner Barbara Moors.

The GenZ series, on which he has been working since 2022, was exhibited at Cri des Lumières in 2024.

GenZ is published by La Belle Étoile*, 160 pages in color, landscape format, 29 x 21 cm, softcover. The book is on sale on the La Belle Étoile* website www.la-belle-etoile.art/shop/p/genz-par-stphane-coutelle

article_text:
Art Review

The Center Cannot Hold at the Toronto Biennial

It’s a provocative and discursive exploration of how artists respond to our late-capitalist epoch, but its focus on “rupture” raises questions.

Hyperallergic )

TORONTO — At the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, this year, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney declared that the world is “in the midst of a rupture, not a transition.” The line is quoted in the catalog for the fourth Toronto Biennial of Art , Things Fall Apart , and could serve as the exhibition’s epigraph.

Curated by Allison Glenn, who spent her childhood in Detroit, crossing into Canada through Windsor, the edition brings together more than 30 artists and collectives across Toronto and, for the first time, sites beyond it, including Anchorage in Alaska and Times Square in New York.

Glenn keeps the Biennial’s long-running focus on water, taking the Great Lakes as her point of departure to ask what artists who work with rupture can teach us about histories, borders, and movement. With Canada–United States relations at an unprecedented low, a cross-border exhibition built around shared waterways feels just right.

The most affecting works treat histories of rupture as an imaginative encounter to be conjured rather than a settled narrative to be recorded. At the Art Gallery of Ontario (AGO), Dawoud Bey’s Material Histories, Living Landscapes hangs photographs from three landscape series tightly together around his two-channel video “350,000” (2023), alongside sculptures and ritual objects from the AGO’s collection with roots in Nigeria, Ghana, and the Kingdom of Kongo. The pairing sets up a striking sonic and visual call and response across the Middle Passage, elucidating the ways the afterlife of slavery permeates the physical world around us. The film’s point-of-view movement through dense woods, accompanied by the sound of heavy breathing and black-and-white images of gnarled landscapes and old homes, suggests that the fight to live free from racial violence is still an urgent one today.

Karachi Biennale Cancels Fifth Edition Over “War Conditions”

The cancellation of the January 2027 event reportedly came without the input of the biennale’s curator, Noor Ahmed.

The Karachi Biennale in Pakistan announced the cancellation of its fifth edition in an Instagram statement on Friday, October 9, citing logistical constraints and uncertainties amid "war conditions prevailing in the region."

Originally scheduled for January 16 through January 31, the biennale was to welcome artists to Karachi, the largest city in Pakistan and the capital of its Sindh province. It is not yet clear what specific circumstances or events in the region contributed to the cancellation, which reportedly occurred without the input of the biennale’s curator, Noor Ahmed , according to the Pakistani newspaper Dawn ’s cultural imprint, Images .

"Artists and partners have been contacting me and they are all quite disappointed about how communications and commitments with them are being handled," Ahmed told Hyperallergic . For the past 13 months, she engaged over 100 artists and practices for the biennale and enlisted three individuals to co-curate sections of the event.

The Karachi Biennale Trust, which organizes the event, has not replied to Hyperallergic 's immediate request for comment.

article_text:
Over the last few days, Lucca Comics and Games , Europe’s largest Comic-Con, has been celebrating its 60th anniversary.

The medieval city located in Italy’s Tuscany region hosted creative leaders, artists and players of games, authors of comic books, manga, showrunners and animators of TV series and anime, actors and directors of films. Around 80,000 ticket-paying fans per day flooded the city and visited the various pavilions, exhibitions and pop-up experiences dotted throughout the city.

Related Stories

Ju Ji-hoon, Choo Young-woo Return for Netflix’s ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call’ Seasons 2 and 3

'PUBG' Live-Action Series From Donald Glover, Stephen Glover in Development at Netflix

Here are five takeaways from this year’s event.

Queues for HBO’s Harry Potter pavilion began in the early morning before crocodiling and winding around the pavilion. Visitors were treated to a peek at props from the show, were given temporary tattoos for the House of their choice and got to see a specially filmed message from John Lithgow and Nick Frost, who play Albus Dumbledore and Hagrid respectively. Given the obvious anticipation of the show, it was a pity that no one from the show was physically present nor were there any previews of footage granted. Many of the fans were cautious in their enthusiasm. A fan of the films, Stefano – who was confusingly dressed as a Jedi – told Variety, “It will be fun to see the books addressed in a way that is deeper.” Alessia, from Lake Como and dressed as Maleficent, worried that “they’ve made too many changes.” Perhaps, the showmakers were worried about such doubts being expressed prior to the show’s release on Christmas Day.

“Percy Jackson and the Olympians” fandom is alive and well, and turned up with a large presence including key cast members Walker Scobell, Leah Sava Jeffries and Aryan Simhadri as well as showrunners Jonathan E. Steinberg and Dan Shotz. Having attended a panel earlier in the day, the cast appeared on a terrace overlooking Piazza della Magione to greet over 8000 fans who had gathered dressed in the colors of Camp Halfblood from the show.

The live-action adaptation of the “Blue Lock” anime and manga series received a European premiere. The film follows an authoritarian regime who have set up a kind of survival game to choose the most selfish (and therefore best) soccer striker from 300 candidates, with the ultimate aim of winning Japan the World Cup. The film is a faithful rendering of its anime predecessor and plays like a demented mix of “Battle Royale” and the Michael Caine soccer pic “Victory.”

The return of Frank Miller (“The Dark Knight Returns,” “Sin City”) meant that comic book royalty continues to show up to greet the fans and announce new works. This time a further collaboration with Peach Momoko, which will explore and be inspired by Japanese horror stories. Also, groundbreaking Japanese manga artist Go Nagai was also feted with a special exhibition entitled “Sun, Heart, and Steel,” featuring his groundbreaking “Mazinger Z,” which inaugurated the Mecha genre, as well as his Devilman, which fittingly enough was inspired by the illustration of Dante’s “Divine Comedy.”

One of the major attractions of Lucca is that provided by the public itself. The dedication and imagination and sheer extravagance of the cosplayers provides the city with a constant rolling panorama of personalities. From the inhabitants of Middle Earth and Hogwarts, to the Mario Bros. and Squid Game, Lucca for a few days becomes a Cosplay Utopia. Spotted among the crowds was “Leon: the Professional” from the 1994 Luc Besson film, complete with silenced pistol and houseplant, a Walter White, a bunch of friends who had come dressed as the cast of the original “Jurassic Park” complete with Jeep. The regular “Star Wars” parade was led by a Mandalorian, who revealed himself to be popular Italian author and television personality Alberto Angela who had spent the day moving through the crowd incognito.

Lucca Comics and Games ran from Oct. 28 to Nov. 1.

article_text:
国立新美術館（東京都港区）から、2027年度の展覧会スケジュールが発表されました。

2027年に開館20周年の節目を迎える国立新美術館。「ディーヴァ展」「国立新美術館 開館20周年記念展（仮称）」「ギルバート＆ジョージ展」「リヒテンシュタイン侯爵家コレクション 西洋美術における古代」と、全部で4つの展覧会を予定。これまでの軌跡を振り返る記念展をはじめ、歴史的な名品や現代の先鋭的な作品の数々と出会い、芸術と社会の関わりを見つめ直す多彩なプログラムが展開されます。

そこでここまで判明した各展覧会の概要について、それぞれまとめました。

国立新美術館

所在地：国立新美術館（東京都港区六本木7-22-2）

開館時間：10:00～18:00 企画展会期中の毎週金・土は20:00まで （入場は閉館の30分前まで）

休館日：毎週火曜日（ただし火曜日が祝日または振替休日の場合は開館し、翌平日に休館）、年末年始

観覧料：展覧会ごとに異なる（詳細は各展の詳細発表を要確認）

アクセス： 東京メトロ千代田線乃木坂駅 青山霊園方面改札6出口（美術館直結） 東京メトロ日比谷線六本木駅 4a出口から徒歩約5分 都営地下鉄大江戸線六本木駅 7出口から徒歩約4分 ※美術館に駐車場はございません

詳細は、 国立新美術館公式サイト まで。

ディーヴァ展

3月24日～7月19日

19世紀から現代にいたるディーヴァの歴史を見つめ、その圧倒的な創造性、社会的な影響力、文化的意義を考察する展覧会です。オペラ、舞台芸術、映画、ポピュラー音楽の世界で活躍してきたパフォーマーたち約100名が取り上げられます。

ディーヴァが実際に身に着けた約60点の貴重な衣装を中心に、写真、映像、雑誌、ポスター、LPなど多彩な作品を通し、フェミニズムの歴史と関連して「ディーヴァ」という概念が時代とともにどのように変化してきたかを探ります。「歌声」に包まれる特別な鑑賞体験も本展ならではの魅力です。

国立新美術館 開館20周年記念展（仮称）

4月21日～7月26日

2007年の開館以来20周年の節目を迎える国立新美術館が、これまで開催した全140に及ぶ展覧会の中で紹介してきたアーティストの試みに光が当てられます。世界のことわりを示す6つの疑問詞―who,where,when,what,how,why―をキーワードに、19世紀から現代まで、様々な時代においてアートの枠組みを広げてきた表現を見つめ直し、絶え間ない変化の中にある多様で複雑な世界を映し出す珠玉の作品が紹介されます。本展の出品作品はすべて全国の国立美術館が長い時間をかけて収蔵を続けてきた作品からのハイライトでもあります。

ギルバート＆ジョージ展

9月17日～12月20日

英国ロンドンを拠点に「Art for All（すべての人にアートを）」を追求するギルバート＆ジョージの活動に焦点が当てられます。自らを「生きる彫刻」と称し、全身に多彩色メタリックの顔料を塗りテーブル上でミュージック・ホールの定番曲を歌って踊る傑作《歌う彫刻》の映像から、宗教やセクシャリティ、都市生活などをテーマにした近年の巨大な写真グループ「ピクチャーズ」までが一挙に展観されます。

リヒテンシュタイン侯爵家コレクション 西洋美術における古代

9月8日～12月6日

上記で紹介した「ギルバート＆ジョージ展」とほぼ同時期に開催されます。国立新美術館でリヒテンシュタイン侯爵家のコレクションをテーマとした展覧会が開催されるのは、2012年10月3日～12月23日まで開催された「リヒテンシュタイン 華麗なる侯爵家の秘宝」以来、約15年ぶりとなります。現時点では詳細は明らかにされていませんが、今回は「古代」に焦点が当てられるということで、今からどんな作品が来日するのか非常に楽しみです。

開館20周年という大きな節目を迎える2027年の国立新美術館では、これまでの歩みと全国の国立美術館の至宝を結集させた記念展をはじめ、時代を切り拓いてきた表現者たちのエネルギーに満ちた展覧会が目白押しです。世界的な歌姫たちの創造性とフェミニズムの歩みを辿る「ディーヴァ展」、半世紀以上にわたり社会や人間を独自の視点で捉え続けてきたユニットの真髄に迫る「ギルバート＆ジョージ展」、そして優美なる歴史の精華を堪能できる「リヒテンシュタイン侯爵家コレクション」など、いずれも見逃せない充実のラインナップとなっています。驚きと意外性に満ちた展覧会を手掛け続けてきた国立新美術館の2027年は、記念イヤーにふさわしい新たな芸術の魅力と出会える特別な1年となりそうです。（美術展ナビ）
